rows.title: Hephaestus's golden attendants in the Iliad
rows.description: In Book 18 of the Iliad, the smith-god Hephaestus is helped by maidens made of gold who can move, think, and speak. They are among the earliest literary images of crafted servants with minds.
rows.why_it_matters: Long before R.U.R., Homer imagines crafted servants who think and speak, showing that the dream of made minds is tied from the start to the dream of tireless labor.
rows.check_note: Composition late 8th to early 7th century BCE; c. 750 is a placement, not a date.
rows.place_label: Ionia: Smyrna (İzmir) or Chios, by tradition
rows.place_note: No place of composition is known. Ancient tradition made Homer a blind bard from Ionia; Pindar named Chios and Smyrna. Drawn at Smyrna as a placement for the Ionian tradition, not a fact.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Homer': 'the most widespread that he was a blind bard from Ionia'; Pindar: 'Homer originated from Chios and Smyrna'; all accounts 'historically apocryphal'.
rows.speaks_note: Iliad 18: the golden attendants have intelligence, voice, and strength (per the use-case 03 description).
rows.geo_match: İzmir, Konak, Izmir, Aegean Region, 35250, Turkey

rows.title: Confucius (attributed), Analects
rows.date_display: Warring States period (475–221 BCE), final form in the Han dynasty
rows.who: Disciples and later followers of Confucius
rows.description: The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges between Confucius and his disciples, assembled after his death. Its question-and-answer form makes ethical teaching an act of conversation between teacher and student.
rows.why_it_matters: The Analects frames moral teaching as exchange between teacher and student, a useful contrast with Plato and a precursor to thinking about how an assistant is trained through guided interaction.
rows.check_note: Scholarly consensus: compiled over the Warring States period (475–221 BCE), reaching final form in the mid-Han dynasty. The draft's 5th–3rd century range was close; the Han final form was missing. The Legge quotation of 1.1 matches the Gutenberg text exactly.
rows.quote: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?
rows.quote_attribution: Analects 1.1, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861)
rows.place_label: Qufu, in the state of Lu
rows.place_note: Compiled and edited by disciples after Confucius's death in 479 BCE, over the Warring States period; Confucius was born in Zou, in modern Qufu, in Lu, and taught there. Where the compilation happened is not recorded.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Analects' ('collected and jointly edited by the disciples after Confucius' death in 479 BCE'); 'Confucius' ('born ... in Zou (陬, in modern Qufu, Shandong)').
rows.speaks_note: No made being; a record of conversation.
rows.geo_match: Qufu City, Jining, Shandong, China

rows.title: Plato, Phaedrus
rows.description: In this dialogue Socrates and the young Phaedrus walk outside the walls of Athens and discuss love, rhetoric, and the soul. Near its end Socrates tells the myth of Theuth and Thamus, a critique of writing as a text that cannot answer back when it is questioned.
rows.why_it_matters: Socrates complains that written words cannot answer questions, a challenge that chatbots seem to answer and one the seminar can test against Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson on turn-taking.
rows.check_note: Composition c. 370 BCE confirmed. The draft said the dialogue 'closes with' the myth of Theuth and Thamus; the myth comes near the end (274c), and the dialogue closes with a prayer to Pan.
rows.place_label: Athens: the Academy; the dialogue is set by the Ilissos outside the walls
rows.place_note: Plato wrote most of the dialogues at the Academy in Athens between 383 and 366 BCE; the conversation itself takes place by a stream under a plane tree outside the city.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Plato': 'From 383 BC until about 366 BC, Plato primarily spent his time at the Academy, writing the majority of the dialogues'; 'Phaedrus (dialogue)': 'They sit by a stream under a plane tree and a chaste tree'.
rows.speaks_note: The made thing here is writing itself, which Socrates says 'cannot answer' when questioned (275d).

rows.title: Talos in the Argonautica
rows.description: In Book 4 of the Argonautica, Medea defeats Talos, the man of bronze who guards Crete. She does so by draining the single vein that carries his life.
rows.why_it_matters: Talos is a bronze guardian bound to a task and undone through a single weakness, an early picture of made beings as workers and of their vulnerability.
rows.check_note: Argonautica confirmed as 3rd century BCE. The draft called Talos a 'bronze giant'; the Talos article notes that no ancient source says he was a giant.
rows.place_label: Alexandria (Apollonius's library post); the myth sets Talos on Crete
rows.place_note: Apollonius was a pupil of Callimachus and held a post at the Library of Alexandria; the Lives say he redrafted the poem at Rhodes. The bronze guardian himself belongs to Crete.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Apollonius of Rhodes' (Alexandria librarian; 'redrafted the Argonautica ... at Rhodes'); 'Talos' ('protected Crete from pirates and invaders').
rows.speaks_note: In Apollonius Talos hurls boulders at the Argo; no speech is recorded.
rows.geo_match: Alexandria, 21519, Egypt

rows.title: Pygmalion in Ovid's Metamorphoses
rows.description: In Book 10 of the Metamorphoses, the sculptor Pygmalion falls in love with an ivory woman he has carved. Venus brings her to life.
rows.why_it_matters: Pygmalion's statue shows the desire for a made figure indistinguishable from a person, a fantasy of creation that Shelley and Wilde later complicate.
rows.check_note: Metamorphoses dated 8 CE.
rows.place_note: Ovid had completed the Metamorphoses by 8 CE, the year he was banished from Rome to Tomis. Wikipedia does not say where he wrote it; Rome is inferred from his residence until exile.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Ovid': 'By AD 8, Ovid had completed Metamorphoses'; 'In AD 8, Ovid was banished to Tomis'.
rows.speaks_note: The ivory statue comes to life; Ovid gives her no words.

rows.title: Yan Shi's artificial man in the Liezi
rows.date_display: c. 4th century CE (approximate compilation of the text)
rows.description: A Daoist text tells how the artificer Yan Shi presents King Mu of Zhou with a lifelike performing man built of leather, wood, and lacquer. The king grows angry when the figure flirts with his concubines, and Yan Shi takes it apart to show it is artificial.
rows.why_it_matters: The king mistakes a mechanical performer for a living man until it is dismantled, an early story of passing as human and of anger at being fooled.
rows.check_note: Current text probably compiled around the 4th century CE (attributed to Zhang Zhan).
rows.place_label: Jiankang (Nanjing), capital of the Eastern Jin, under which the received text was compiled
rows.place_note: All received Liezi texts derive from Zhang Zhan's edition (c. 370 CE), made under the Eastern Jin, whose capital was Jiankang. Zhang's own whereabouts are not recorded; the tale itself is set centuries earlier at the court of King Mu of Zhou.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Liezi': 'All received Liezi texts derive from Zhang's version'; 'Eastern Jin': capital 'Jiankang (modern Nanjing)', 317–420.
rows.speaks_note: In the tale the artificial man sings in tune and dances; whether it speaks is not stated in the sources opened.
rows.geo_match: Nanjing City, Jiangsu, China

rows.title: Rava creates a man (Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b)
rows.date_display: c. 500–550 CE (redaction of the Babylonian Talmud; Sanhedrin 65b)
rows.description: In a brief Talmudic passage, the sage Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira. The figure cannot speak, and Rabbi Zeira returns him to dust; this is a founding text for later golem traditions.
rows.why_it_matters: Rava's made man cannot speak and is turned back to dust, tying the creation of a being to the question of whether speech signals a mind.
rows.check_note: Sanhedrin 65b (Rava creates a man and sends him to Rav Zeira) confirmed. Wikipedia says the traditional c. 500 CE compilation date is probably early; the middle of the sixth century is more likely.

rows.title: Al-Jazari's Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
rows.description: The engineer al-Jazari described and illustrated water clocks, humanoid servants, and a boat of musical automata in a treatise for the Artuqid court. The work is a landmark in the history of programmable mechanism.
rows.why_it_matters: Al-Jazari's servant figures and musical automata show real engineering of machines that perform human tasks, grounding the seminar's literary made beings in actual mechanism.
rows.check_note: Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, 1206.

rows.speaks_note: Drink-serving and musical automata; birds that sing. No speaking device.

rows.title: Legend of Albertus Magnus's talking head
rows.date_display: 13th century (period of the legend's subject; recorded later)
rows.description: Later medieval and early modern stories claimed that the scholar Albertus Magnus built a speaking head or android. In the legend, his pupil Thomas Aquinas destroyed it.
rows.why_it_matters: The legend of a speaking head built by a scholar and then destroyed by his pupil shows long-standing anxiety about talking machines and the limits of human making.
rows.check_note: A legend recorded after Albertus's lifetime; the 13th-century placement is for his life, not the legend's first telling.
rows.place_label: Cologne (legend; the sources name no place)
rows.place_note: The brazen-head legend attaches to Albertus Magnus but names no city; Cologne, where he taught and died in 1280, is used as a placement. Wikipedia's article on Albertus does not mention the legend at all.

rows.title: Vaucanson exhibits the Flute Player
rows.description: Vaucanson showed a life-size automaton that played the flute by controlling breath and finger movements. The following year he added the famous Digesting Duck.
rows.why_it_matters: Vaucanson's flute player made audiences ask whether a machine's lifelike performance was real skill or clever illusion, a debate that anticipates later talk about imitation and testing.
rows.check_note: Built 1737; presented to the Académie des Sciences in early 1738.
rows.place_note: Presented to the Académie des Sciences in early 1738.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Jacques de Vaucanson': 'in early 1738, he presented his creation to the Académie des Sciences'.
rows.speaks_note: It plays the flute; none of Vaucanson's automata spoke.

rows.title: The Mechanical Turk
rows.description: Kempelen unveiled a chess-playing automaton dressed as a Turk, which toured Europe and America for decades. It was a hoax worked by a hidden human player.
rows.why_it_matters: The Turk is a founding hoax of machine intelligence: people judged a mind by its moves and never saw the human hidden inside, which anticipates later worries about passing as human.
rows.check_note: First displayed 1770.
rows.place_note: Debut in 1770 at Schönbrunn Palace; Kempelen's home was Pressburg (Bratislava). A voice box saying 'Échec!' was added only after Mälzel bought it in 1805.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Mechanical Turk': 'The Turk made its debut in 1770 at Schönbrunn Palace'; 'A voice box was added following the Turk's acquisition by Mälzel'.
rows.speaks_note: Silent at its debut; one word ('Échec!') after 1805, and a human inside throughout.

rows.title: Jaquet-Droz's The Writer
rows.description: The Swiss watchmaker Pierre Jaquet-Droz built a boy automaton that writes a programmable text of up to about forty characters with a quill. It belongs to a set with a draughtsman and a musician that survives in Neuchâtel.
rows.why_it_matters: A programmable automaton that writes lets seminar members ask early on who the author is when a machine produces text, a question that returns with Wilde and with chatbots.
rows.check_note: The three automata were built between 1768 and 1774.
rows.place_note: The three automata were presented at La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1774 according to the Jaquet Droz company history; the Wikipedia article says only that they are now in the Musée d'Art et d'Histoire, Neuchâtel.
rows.opened: Wikipedia 'Jaquet-Droz automata' (built 1768–1774; kept in Neuchâtel); web search summary of jaquet-droz.com ('presented in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1774').

rows.description: A bellows, a reed, and a leather mouth worked by hand to produce words and short sentences. Kempelen began it in 1769 and described it in a 456-page book with 27 plates, published in Vienna in 1791: the first machine built to speak, as opposed to play or write.

rows.title: "The Sandman"
rows.description: The student Nathanael falls in love with Olimpia, who turns out to be an automaton, and he descends into madness. Freud later made the story central to his essay on the uncanny.
rows.why_it_matters: Nathanael takes an automaton for a listener who understands him, a story about projecting mind onto a made companion and a precursor to the uncanny quality of talking machines.

rows.title: Mary Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
rows.description: Victor Frankenstein, a young natural philosopher, assembles a living being and then abandons it. The creature learns language and argues its case to its maker, and the story is framed by a chain of letters and nested narrations.
rows.why_it_matters: The creature is made, abandoned, taught language, and then argues with its maker, which frames the seminar's questions about responsibility, upbringing, and what we owe the beings we build.

rows.date_display: April 1836 (publication in the Southern Literary Messenger)
rows.description: Poe published an essay arguing that the touring chess automaton must be operated by a concealed human. He reasoned from the machine's behavior to the necessity of a mind inside it.

rows.description: A watchmaker spends years building a delicate mechanical butterfly that seems alive. When it is crushed, the story turns the loss into a meditation on art and spirit.

rows.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
rows.description: LoRA introduced a way to customize large pretrained models by training a comparatively tiny set of additional parameters rather than modifying the entire model.
